article_text:
Three suspects in Sunday’s shooting at Bollywood action star Tiger Shroff ’s car have been taken into custody in Kota, in the northwestern state of Rajasthan, according to local media.

Reports differ on whether the men have been formally arrested or only detained. Police have not publicly named them or confirmed that they fired the shots.

The men were picked up in Kota’s Railway Colony area on Monday, local media reported. Investigators believe the attackers had scouted Shroff’s routine. They reportedly knew he played soccer in Juhu on Sundays and waited around 45 minutes outside the ground before opening fire as he walked back to his car. They then rode a Pulsar motorcycle along SV Road and abandoned it outside Andheri West railway station before catching a train toward Borivali, ANI reported. Preliminary intelligence had suggested they crossed into Gujarat.

Police have registered a case against three unidentified men on charges including attempted murder and conspiracy, along with offenses under the Arms Act. Mumbai Police set up 15 teams to hunt the attackers, and the Crime Branch has taken over the investigation. Forensic teams gathered spent cartridges at the scene.

Popular on Variety

The shooting took place around 7 p.m. on Sunday near Pushpa Park in Mumbai’s western suburb of Juhu, as Shroff drove away from a soccer session. Several reports say the attackers arrived on a motorcycle and fled after firing. Police initially put the number of rounds at three or four. Maharashtra’s deputy chief minister, Eknath Shinde, who visited the family on Sunday night, said five were fired.

Shroff avoided being hit. According to Shinde, the actor’s hands were hurt by gunpowder and flying glass. Reports said his driver, Firdaus, was struck in the left arm by a bullet and is stable, and that an autorickshaw driver named Chauhan was also hurt. The two men were treated at Vile Parle’s Nanavati Hospital. Shroff and his family have not commented publicly.

Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis phoned the actor. “We are all with you. We will track down the accused soon. Do not worry,” Fadnavis told Shroff, according to local media. He also sought a full report from Mumbai Police Commissioner Deven Bharti. Opposition parties have accused his government of failing to keep order in the city.

A social media post purportedly from the Lawrence Bishnoi gang says it carried out the attack and identifies the men behind it as Anil Pandit, a gang member, and Harman Sandhu. In an audio clip shared online, a man calling himself Pandit said Shroff had been singled out for defying the gang and continuing to work with Bollywood superstar Salman Khan, and he threatened anyone in the industry who works with the star. Police have not verified either claim, and no motive has been established.

The All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) placed the shooting alongside earlier attacks on film figures, including gunfire outside the homes of Salman Khan and filmmaker Rohit Shetty, the January 2025 knife attack on Saif Ali Khan inside his home and the repeated targeting of comedian Kapil Sharma’s cafe. Police said at the time that Saif Ali Khan was attacked by an intruder during an attempted break-in.

Gangsters want to “terrorize Bollywood personalities and extort money from them,” AICWA president Suresh Shyamlal Gupta said in a statement. “Today it is Tiger Shroff. Who is next?”

The association urged the state to arrest both the shooters and those who sent them, dismantle the extortion network and give film personalities and their families protection. The Federation of Western India Cine Employees (FWICE) also condemned the attack and called for an investigation that is “thorough, impartial and time-bound.”

The gang’s feud with Salman Khan dates to 1998, when the actor was accused of killing two blackbucks, an antelope the Bishnoi community holds sacred, during the Rajasthan shoot of “Hum Saath Saath Hain.” He was convicted by a trial court in 2018 and has appealed. In April 2024, two men on a motorcycle fired five rounds outside his Galaxy Apartments home in Bandra, and five suspects allegedly tied to the gang are now on trial. Six months later, politician Baba Siddique was shot dead in Bandra, a killing a suspected conspirator attributed to the gang online. In February, gunfire hit Shetty’s Juhu home, and the gang later claimed it.

The 36-year-old’s father is veteran star Jackie Shroff. Shroff broke through with 2014’s “Heropanti” and has since led the “Baaghi” action franchise and starred opposite Hrithik Roshan in Yash Raj Films’ “War.”

"与德尔·托罗一同出席的还有电影节总监丹妮拉·米歇尔（Daniela Michel）、《潘神的迷宫》制片人伯莎·纳瓦罗（Bertha Navarro）、当年年轻的主演伊万娜·巴克罗（Ivana Baquero）以及摄影指导吉尔莫·纳瓦罗（Guillermo Navarro），后者曾凭借这部反法西斯寓言中惊艳的摄影作品斩获奥斯卡最佳摄影奖。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在回应记者会上中途提出的一关于自《潘神的迷宫》上映20年来有哪些保持不变、哪些发生了变化的问题时，德尔·托罗潸然泪下。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“当今我们物种和社会的现状，超出了我们当年所能想象的任何极限。但我认出了同样的悲伤与绝望。看到一代、两代或三代人辜负了下一代，我感到痛彻心扉。我们留给后代的是一个满目疮痍、在道德、社会和精神上支离破碎的世界，曾经让我们得以讲述寓言和比喻的肌理正在分崩离析。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当被问及事前是否知道《潘神的迷宫》会广受欢迎时，德尔·托罗回忆了与两位纳瓦罗的合作如何支撑他度过了他们所面临的所有挑战。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他说：“我们踏上了一场在经济上令人心惊肉跳、但在电影美学上却无比美丽的冒险。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“你永远不知道一部电影会受到怎样的反响。直到我们在戛纳第一次放映时才知晓。我们赢得了长达22分钟以上的著名全场起立鼓掌，从那一刻起，一切都变了。它改变了我们的人生。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我认为《潘神的迷宫》对我的意义是一个分水岭。在创作自由、可能性以及其他一切方面，我能有今天全拜这部电影所赐。但如果没有我的直系亲属、伯莎和吉尔莫的信任，这一切都是不可能做到的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "摄影指导纳瓦罗表示：“吉尔莫和我有着共同的信念，即电影语言是通过传递情感与叙事的影像来讲述故事。《潘神的迷宫》便是这一理念的极致表达。镜头在不断地搜寻、发现与交流。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“这也是一次极其艰难的拍摄。我们的预算有限，必须寻找非传统的解决方案，并冒着极易失败的风险。但我们赌赢了。毫无疑问，这是我最好的电影，这段经历常驻我心。我希望新一代人能继续发现并欣赏它。而现在，20年过去了，它归来了。万岁（Olé）！”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "曾支持德尔·托罗开启职业生涯的长片处女作《鬼童院》及广受赞誉的《潘神的迷宫》的制片人纳瓦罗表示：“当他把《鬼童院》的剧本交给我时，我完全被迷住了。才华会发光，而你必须懂得去识别那种光芒。这就是我在吉尔莫身上看到的。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“能与吉尔莫共同创作那三部伟大的电影，是难以置信的荣幸。我一生中制作过许多电影，但这三部对我有着更深远的意义。它们改变了我的人生。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "巴克罗表示赞同：“《潘神的迷宫》毫无疑问为我打开了通往类型片和职业生涯的大门。我们今天下午一直在讨论这部电影如何在职业和个人层面上改变了我们的人生。对我来说，表演从一种爱好——在拍《潘神的迷宫》之前我曾工作过——变成了我的职业。如果没有那部电影，我今天可能就不会站在这里。它毫无疑问地标志着我职业生涯的转折点。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在谈到该片对年轻观众的影响时，德尔·托罗指出：“《潘神的迷宫》中并存着一种紧迫感、脆弱性与凶猛性。不知为何，我认为这是一个迫切的时刻，需要让这部电影去跟新一代观众对话。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "地方政治也渗入了这场记者会，一名记者问他，对于家乡瓜达拉哈拉的年轻人因水污染、镇压以及10月11日抗议者遭涉嫌绑架等当前问题而进行的抗议，他有什么想对他们说的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他回应道：“今天上午在我的大师班上，我把发言的机会交给了年轻人，让他们谈论这些问题。令人感到骇人的是，如此基本的事情竟然需要去争取，而不是通过最基本的人性与负责任的领导力来解决。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我曾明确表态：‘必须听取他们的心声，我100%支持他们。’问题迟迟得不到解决，或者有人试图让其噤声，这是不可接受的。发声、抗议并要求得到解决方案是基本的权利——在任何时间、任何地点。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "莫雷利亚国际电影节于10月16日开幕，并于10月25日闭幕。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Mexico’s beloved Guillermo del Toro descended on the 24 th Morelia Film Festival like the rockstar he is, greeted by hordes of shrieking fans that impressed even the most jaded in the crowd.

In town to present the much-anticipated 3D Re-Release of “Pan’s Labyrinth,” he was everywhere all at once, holding a masterclass where tickets were as elusive as a seat at Cannes that went on for nearly three hours and a free-wheeling press conference that extended past its time limit.

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

It was his third time at the fest, 20 years after his multi-Oscar winning “Pan’s Labyrinth’ first played there and years later with his 2018 best picture Academy Award winner “The Shape of Water.”

Before the presser kicked off, Del Toro, an Honorary Doctorate recipient from the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM), received the Filmoteca UNAM Medal, an honor also bestowed on Alfonso Cuarón, in town to support his son Jonas Cuarón’s opening night film, “Campeón Gabacho,” which he produced.

Alongside Del Toro were festival director Daniela Michel, “Pan’s Labyrinth” producer Bertha Navarro, his then young lead Ivana Baquero and DP Guillermo Navarro, who took home the cinematography Oscar for his stunning work on the anti-fascist fable.

Reflecting on a question posed midway through the press conference about what has stayed the same and what has changed over the 20 years since “Pan’s Labyrinth,” del Toro responded with tears.

“The state of our species and society today goes beyond anything we could have imagined back then. But I recognize the same sadness and despair. It pains me deeply to see one, two, or three generations fail the next. We’re handing down a world in ruins, morally, socially and spiritually fractured, with the very fabric that once allowed us to tell fables and parables falling apart.”

Asked whether he knew beforehand if “Pan’s Labyrinth” would be well received, Del Toro recounted how his collaborations with both Navarros sustained him through all the challenges they faced.

“We embarked on an adventure that was financially horrifying but cinematically beautiful,” he said.

“You never know how a film will be received. We only found out when we screened it for the first time at Cannes. We got that famous standing ovation that lasted more than 22 minutes, and from that moment on, everything changed. It changed our lives.”

“I think ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ marked a before and after for me. In terms of creative freedom, possibilities and everything else, I’m where I am today because of that film. But none of it would have been possible without the faith of my immediate family, Bertha and Guillermo.”

Said DP Navarro: “Guillermo and I share the belief that cinematic language is storytelling through images that convey emotion and narrative. ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ is the ultimate expression of that. The camera is constantly searching, discovering and communicating.”

“It was also an incredibly difficult shoot. We had a limited budget, had to find unconventional solutions and took risks that could easily have failed. But we gambled and we won. Without a doubt, it’s my best film, and I hold that experience close to my heart. I hope new generations will continue to discover and appreciate it. And now, 20 years later, it returns. Olé!”

Producer Navarro, who also backed Del Toro’s career-launching feature debut “Cronos” and his much-lauded “The Devil’s Backbone,” said: “When he gave me the screenplay for ‘Cronos,’ I was absolutely fascinated. Talent shines, and you have to know how to recognize that light. That’s what I saw in Guillermo.”

“It’s been an incredible privilege to have made those three great films with Guillermo. I’ve produced many films throughout my life, but those three hold a much deeper significance for me. They changed my life.”

Baquero concurred: “’Pan’s Labyrinth’ undoubtedly opened doors for me, both into the genre and in my career. We’ve talked this afternoon about how much the film changed our lives, professionally and personally. For me, acting went from being a hobby – I had worked before ‘Pan’s Labyrinth’ – to becoming my profession. Without that film, I might not be here today. It unquestionably marked a turning point in my career.”

Reflecting on its impact on young audiences. Del Toro noted: “There’s an urgency and a fragility and ferocity that coexist in ‘Pan’s Labyrinth.’ And somehow, I think it’s an urgent moment to speak, for the film to speak to a new audience.”

Local politics also crept into the conference, with a journalist asking him what he would say to the young people protesting in his hometown of Guadalajara over its current issues of contaminated water, repression and the alleged kidnapping of protesters on Oct. 11.

He responded: “This morning at my masterclass, I gave young people the floor to speak about these issues. It’s terrifying that something so fundamental should have to be fought for instead of being resolved through basic humanity and responsible leadership.”

“I said it clearly: “Their voices must be heard, and I stand with them 100%. It’s unacceptable that this remains unresolved or that anyone would try to silence them. Speaking out, protesting, and demanding a solution are fundamental rights – anytime, anywhere.”

The Morelia Film Festival began on Oct. 16 and wraps Oct. 25.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: The AFI Silver Theatre and Cultural Center will open the 39th edition of its European Union Film Showcase with Ryūsuke Hamaguchi ’s Paris-set feature All Of A Sudden . Scroll down for the full list of titles.

The 2026 AFI European Union Film Showcase runs from December 2–20 at the American Film Institute’s historic theatre in Silver Spring, Maryland. This year’s showcase features 57 films representing all 27 EU member states, including 25 of the top contenders for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film.

The slate of titles features award winners like Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudden, which won Best Actress for its two leads at Cannes, alongside regional box-office hits, debut works by up-and-coming talents and new works by leading auteurs.

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

Gotham Awards Film Nominations Led By 'The Invite', 'Tender Loving Care', 'All Of A Sudden' & More

AFI Fest Opens Tonight: President & CEO Bob Gazzale On Why It Matters In The Oscar-Season Deluge Of Film Festivals - The Deadline Interview

Described as “a life-affirming tale about the resilience and patience required to truly care for another human being,” All Of A Sudden stars Virginie Efira and Tao Okamoto as a pair of unlikely friends who, after a spontaneous encounter, quickly develop a deep and abiding intimacy. Hamaguchi’s French-language debut is Japan’s Oscar submission for Best International Feature.

The closing night title is Asghar Farhadi’s Parallel Tales. The French-language drama is an ambitious reworking of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s A Short Film About Love and A Short Film About Killing . Starring are Isabelle Huppert, Virginie Efira, Vincent Cassel, Pierre Niney, Adam Bessa, and Catherine Deneuve. The film follows Sylvie (Huppert), a famous author seeking inspiration by observing neighbors across the street. The film premiered at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival and has its North American Premiere at AFI Fest.

Additional highlights from this year’s showcase include La Bola Negra , the buzzy feature from Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi; Florian Zeller’s Bunker , starring Javier Bardem and Penélope Cruz; Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur , which is France’s Oscar submission; and Lukas Dhont’s Coward .

Cultural and community partners of this year’s showcase include Alliance Française of Washington DC, the Austrian Cultural Forum, the Delegation of the European Union to the United States, the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany, the Embassy of the Republic of Poland, the Embassy of Spain, the Embassy of Sweden, and the Italian Cultural Institute.

See the 2026 Showcase titles below. They have been split into films from the Best International Oscar race and other special presentations.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 在柏林KW当代艺术研究所，埃及艺术家拉菲克·格赖斯呈现了“The City and the City”，对时间、期待以及记忆和历史之间不确定关系展开了探索。2026年10月19日 What […]
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "在柏林KW当代艺术研究所，埃及艺术家拉菲克·格赖斯呈现了“The City and the City”，对时间、期待以及记忆和历史之间不确定关系展开了探索。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://artafricamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Rafik_Greiss_website_banner_desktop-1030x447.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "ART AFRICA", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当时间似乎停滞不前时会发生什么？在“The City and the City”中，埃及艺术家拉菲克·格赖斯审视了记忆、感知与生活经验之间的空间，邀请观众重新思考过去如何继续塑造现在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为他的首个机构个人展览，该展汇集了电影和黑白摄影作品，探讨图像如何保存、扭曲和重构经验的碎片。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "展览的核心是一部新委托创作的电影，描绘了栖息在广袤沙漠景观中的神秘人物。当他们观看并等待一个可能永远不会发生的事件时，期待变成了一种劳作，将看似空旷的环境转化为充满心理张力的空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在音乐人7038634357创作的原声音乐伴随下，这部电影从银幕延伸至整个展览空间。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一系列描绘孤立物体、人工制品和废弃地点的照片进一步探究了记忆的不稳定性。这些图像脱离了可识别的地理和历史背景，抵制固定的解读，并鼓励观众构建自己的联想。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由埃玛·恩德比（Emma Enderby）和利伯蒂·阿德里安（Liberty Adrien）策展，“The City and the City”思考了个人回忆与集体历史如何交织，展现了那些未被看见、未得解决或半梦半醒的记忆所蕴含的种种可能。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该展览目前正在柏林KW当代艺术研究所展出，展期至2027年1月10日。", "links": [{"text": "KW Institute for Contemporary Art", "url": "https://www.kw-berlin.de/en/exhibitions/rafik-greiss-the-city-and-the-city"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
At KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin, Egyptian artist Rafik Greiss presents ‘The City and the City’, an exploration of time, anticipation and the uncertain relationship between memory and history.

What happens when time seems to stand still? In ‘The City and the City’, Egyptian artist Rafik Greiss examines the spaces between memory, perception and lived experience, inviting audiences to reconsider how the past continues to shape the present.

Marking his first institutional solo exhibition, the presentation brings together film and black-and-white photography to explore how images preserve, distort, and reconstruct fragments of experience.

At its centre is a newly commissioned film depicting enigmatic figures inhabiting expansive desert landscapes. As they watch and wait for an event that may never occur, anticipation becomes a form of labour, transforming seemingly empty environments into spaces of psychological tension.

Accompanied by a soundtrack composed by musician 7038634357, the film extends beyond the screen into the exhibition space.

A series of photographs depicting isolated objects, artefacts and abandoned places further investigates the instability of memory. Removed from identifiable geographical and historical contexts, these images resist fixed interpretations and encourage viewers to construct their own associations.

Curated by Emma Enderby and Liberty Adrien, ‘The City and the City’ considers how personal recollection and collective history intersect, revealing the possibilities of what remains unseen, unresolved or half-remembered.

This exhibition is on view at the KW Institute for Contemporary Art in Berlin until 10 January 2027.

title_original: ‘Possible Love’ Review: Two Married Couples Begin to Covet Each Others’ Lives in the Latest Stunner from ‘Burning’ Director Lee Chang-dong
editorial_title_zh: 《可能的爱》影评：在《燃烧》导演李沧东的最新惊艳之作中，两对已婚夫妇开始觊觎彼此的生活
editorial_excerpt_zh: 在这部气势恢宏的Netflix剧情片中，阶级冲突展现出鲜活的新维度，故事聚焦于一位富有的纪录片女导演与她的蓝领拍摄对象之间的关系。

"作为现代电影中最具文学气质的作者（他本人也是一位小说家），李沧东的《Possible Love》延续了他作品一贯扣人心弦且兼具小说般多层结构的惊艳质感，这部作品或许是献给克日什托夫·基斯洛夫斯基的《十诫10》的记忆之作，但让我们打消任何将其视为翻拍的想法。本片是独立构思的，随后在前期制作阶段被归入同一个致敬短片合集，该合集以阿斯哈·法哈蒂今年在戛纳带来的糟糕作品《Parallel Tales》开篇；除了李沧东在影片开头赫然呈现在银幕上的那条圣经诫命“不可贪恋”之外，本片与基斯洛夫斯基系列的最后一集没有任何共同之处。", "links": [{"text": "Parallel Tales", "url": "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2266387749-e1793131029947.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "加利福尼亚州洛杉矶 - 3月13日：贾法尔·帕纳西于2026年3月13日在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶的电影艺术与科学学院电影博物馆出席学院博物馆呈献的第98届奥斯卡最佳国际长片提名聚焦活动。（摄影：Arturo Holmes/Getty Images）", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "即便如此，在这部气势恢宏的剧情片中，这一教导的证据却显得捉摸不定。影片围绕两对截然不同的夫妇展开，他们因韩国一家大型金属工厂镇压工人罢工的暴力事件而被拉到了一起。究竟是谁在觊觎什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "影片角色的表面诉求理解起来很简单——至少对女性角色而言是如此。作为一名随性的富有业余爱好者，其苍白的皮肤散发着与她沙龙精修的波波头同样迷人的光泽，新手导演艺智（曹汝贞饰，曾在《寄生虫》中同样饰演富妈妈）希望拍摄一部关于韩国各地劳工状况不断下滑的纪录片，尤其聚焦于一家名为SP重工（SP Heavy Industries）的企业最近发生的动荡。尽管我们看到艺智在向某种资助委员会推介这个项目，但人们推测，她的大部分资金以及全部的创作自由都来自于她那威严雕塑般健美的丈夫相宇（李沧东新片加盟演员赵寅成饰），一个似乎过着毫无摩擦的生活的信托基金男。", "links": [{"text": "Parasite", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/parasite-review-bong-joon-ho-1202143634/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在经济鸿沟的另一端，坚韧却眼神哀伤的美玉（由《密阳》女演员全度妍饰演，在与李沧东首次合作不到20年后的今天，她献出了又一次百年难遇的表演）显然愿意付出任何代价来让她的丈夫重获生机。作为两年前在SP大规模裁员中失去工作和生活目标的“死者”之一，她那沉默寡言、内向压抑的丈夫浩锡（《薄荷糖》主演薛景求饰）自那次导致后续罢工结束的镇压行动中受伤以来，就一直只剩下一个空壳。美玉希望参与艺智的纪录片能让他得以处理自己的创伤——不再像僵尸一样四处游荡，而是重新振作起来，回到她当年作为一个没有任何更好选择的十几岁女裁缝时所爱上的那个男人。希望他能成为他们年幼的儿子哲更称职的父亲，而哲目前毫无方向的状态最好地体现在他极其糟糕的跆拳道水平上。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "抛开这个简单的基准不谈，李沧东和Oh Jung-mi（译名待确认）极为细腻的剧本中运作的欲望矩阵是如此难以捉摸，直到电影第三幕中丝绒般直击心底的最后一幕才真正显露。是的，美玉垂涎艺智优雅的衣橱和设计师手袋，每当她与相宇独处时，空气中总有一种说不清道不明的性张力（这种张力最终在第三幕私人海滩上的一场令人难忘的黎明前戏码中熊熊燃烧）。但如果断定这位工人阶级女性嫉妒她极其富有的新闺蜜，将是愚蠢且过分简化的；同样，如果轻率地认为嫉妒在这部故事中比怨恨扮演了更关键的角色，或者认为像《可能的爱》这样斑驳而深入探究的电影会满足于重新固化韩国富有阶层与贫困阶层之间的鸿沟，也是无济于事的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "李沧东非常乐意激起我们对百分之一富豪的愤怒，而这部电影尖锐的剧本——最初灵感来自于10多年前韩国一家大企业发生的类似事件——在嘲弄艺智如何漫不经心地将自己插入美玉和浩锡的蓝领世界时，表现得最为酣畅淋漓。她想成为他们那个破败的工厂小镇里的一只壁虎（静观其事），但这位养尊处优的纪录片导演却像修道院里的一辆迈巴赫一样格格不入；尽管成长过程中并没有含着金汤匙，但她却为自己无法重新切换代码回到金融阶梯的底层而感到愤怒。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着故事的发展，艺智说服美玉和浩锡在周末加入他们，前往相宇位于国家西海岸的豪华度假屋（这更好地将这对夫妇套牢在她的地盘上，让她可以在一天中的任何时间拍摄他们），李沧东找到了各种狡猾的方式来武器化那个反复出现的视觉笑话：一个亲密场景突然切到艺智正带着相机躲在角落里。令人钦佩的是，她想要突显当所有者阶层为囤积财富而将业务自动化时，工人们是如何被抛在后面的，但艺智却未能意识到她侵犯拍摄对象尊严的种种居高临下的方式，就好像在一个劳动日益从获利者眼中隐形的世界上，像美玉和浩锡这样的人本就该为自己能被看到而感到幸运。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与李沧东气势恢宏、更具爆发力的《燃烧》不同，他在此处讲述的故事建立在一场可怕的暴力事件之上，而非通往暴力事件，但他的最新电影以相似的节奏酝酿至沸腾，同样在长对话场景与不可磨灭的视觉敏锐时刻之间交替。尽管这部相对克制的家庭传奇很难与全钟瑞沿着三八线（DMZ）的夕阳舞蹈相媲美，但李沧东依然保留了他凭空创造奇观的天赋——能将诸如开车回家或去海里简单浸泡这样日常的事情，注入一种压倒性的无声悲情。《Possible Love》中的每一个时刻都如同一场错综复杂的社会经济摩擦交织出的邪恶交响乐般噼啪作响；每一个手势、评论和细节都在雕琢出奇妙的几何形态，这些形态在将这些人拉得更近的同时，也加深了最终将他们隔开的鸿沟。", "links": [{"text": "Burning", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/features/general/burning-lee-chang-dong-steven-yeun-must-see-movie-1202015392/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "有时候，在少数恰到好处的时刻，这种几何形态以一种令人毛骨悚然的方式表现出来。比如：相宇在他的避暑山庄起居室的壁炉架上放了一只古董哨子，而那位常驻的“房屋精灵”——一个似乎不会说话的园丁，过去常和他们小时候一起玩——只要相宇一吹哨子，就被训练得跑过来。然而，在大多数情况下，片中角色之间的距离是以更微妙的方式传达的；体现在相宇挺拔坐姿的自信中、美玉卷发的光泽中，以及浩锡面无表情的直率莫测中——这并非暗示他缺乏内心世界，而是泄露了他不断试图将内心的恶魔压抑住的挣扎。他是痛苦的囚徒，而叶智却像个游客一样轻描淡写地记录着这份痛苦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在《Possible Love》转场至相宇的避暑山庄、迎来这部长达164分钟电影的最后关头时，李沧东对角色身体及其如何承载身体的精心关注获得了巨大的回报（“这就像一本我没读过的小说里的房子，”美玉在晚餐时惊叹道）。在一夜醉酒卡拉OK和在宅邸私人海滩上的几次黎明前漫步之间，电影对自由与权力的金钱驱动型探索开始呈现出更多的身体维度，这种转变有可能扰乱原本将每个人束缚在其角色中的动态；正是在这里，全度妍夺回了控制权，她那生动而大理石般的表演达到了一种极为原始的自我保护状态，以至于让其他角色都失去了知觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/possible-Love_Still_R30_AAA08350_RT2.jpeg?w=650", "alt": "《Possible Love》（从左至右）饰浩锡的薛景求、饰美玉的全度妍剧照。版权所有：Joo Jae-bum/Netflix © 2026", "caption": "《可能的爱》 Netflix", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Possible Love》以绝妙——甚至令人不安——的乐趣拉平了其两对夫妇之间的竞争环境，但那些游移不定的纵容却充斥着现实分量，让人感觉不像是某种愿望成真。这部电影并不天真到去假装其“贫穷”角色能够与富有角色实现真正的平衡，也没有居高临下地暗示被晚期资本主义的冷漠所剥削本身带有某种隐含的尊严。浩锡并非一个神圣的受难者，他是一个深受打击且满腹苦涩的男人，他的困境诉说着反抗一个旨在践踏他这样的人的系统的无望，而李沧东对描绘他的痛苦远比“解决”他的痛苦更感兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Possible Love》的终极力量在影片结束后仍在心中滋长（并且极大地回报任何重复观看），它既不扎根于肆意的绝望，也不扎根于虚假的乐观。尽管浸润在工人阶级的悲伤与挫败之中，李沧东的这部戏剧还是利用其戏中戏的结构，通过人们通过工作实际赚得的东西这一棱镜，折射出劳动的道德价值。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "叶智在朝着自己成为叙事电影制片人的梦想迈进的同时，却在纪录片领域自甘堕落（“想象事物是我的爱好”或许并不是你想从一个指导你生活纪录片的导演口中听到的话），她成了自己二手富裕的受害人——她那顺遂的人生使得她必须通过表演性的“体验派表演”来接近拍摄对象并拍摄任何真实的东西。她的观察手法是对无形劳动的一种讽刺，而这种无形劳动是她第一次在卡塔尔的豪华酒店旅行时抱怨注意到的；然而，若非她为摄像机设计了一个场景让这些人存在，她甚至都看不见美玉和浩锡这样的人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "就相宇而言，他的工作顺风顺水，以至于他可以一边喝着拿铁，一边通过笔记本电脑买卖整个公司，他与叶智的婚姻感觉就像是压了一层塑料膜。他们在一片短暂的争吵中被动地互相挑刺，以免把床单弄脏，并将他们所有的潜意识欲望降级到富人制造的盲区中，这样他们就不用去看自己财富之外的世界了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "相比之下，美玉和浩锡别无选择，只能直面降临在他们身上的苦难，他们对事物的渴望如此强烈，以至于从未忽视彼此付出的心血。他们的人生建立在一种可能的爱之上，因为他们没有奢侈的资本去假装存在其他任何形式的爱。是的，他们的过往——在一系列精雕细琢的闪回中徐徐展开——笨拙而不完美，他们对未来的财务前景也最多只能算得上脆弱，但他们永远不必去觊觎这个世界依然免费施舍给人们的东西。在美玉和浩锡的感觉中，月光仿佛只在夜里为他们而照耀，这部细腻动人、层次惊艳的戏剧在最后关头颂扬了他们为彼此赋予的自由，将那皎洁的光芒永远留给了他们自己。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "评级：A", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Possible Love》在 2026 年威尼斯电影节上首映。Netflix 将于 10 月 23 日星期五将其在院线上映，并于 11 月 6 日星期五上线 Netflix。", "translated": true}]

Netflix will release “ Possible Love ” in theaters on Friday, October 23 before it streams beginning on November 6.]", "links": [{"text": "Venice", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/venice/"}, {"text": "Film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}, {"text": "Possible Love", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/possible-love/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Another heart-stopping and novelistically layered stunner from modern cinema’s most literary auteur (a fiction author himself), Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” might be dedicated to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10,” but let’s dispel any notion of it being a remake. Conceived independently, and then lumped during pre-production into the same tribute omnibus that kicked off with Asghar Farhadi’s dreadful “ Parallel Tales ” at Cannes this year this film shares nothing in common with the final episode of Kieślowski’s series beyond the biblical commandment that Lee splays on screen at the very start: “Thou shalt not covet.”", "links": [{"text": "Parallel Tales", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/criticism/movies/parallel-tales-movie-review-asghar-farhadi-1235193969/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B2289.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "Felipe Bustos Sierra at IndieWire Art of the Doc 2026 held at Lumen on October 19, 2026 in Los Angeles, California.", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/GettyImages-2266387749-e1793131029947.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "LOS ANGELES, CALIFORNIA - MARCH 13: Jafar Panahi attends The Academy Museum Presents 98th Oscars Nominee Spotlight - International Feature Film at Academy Museum of Motion Pictures on March 13, 2026 in Los Angeles, California. article_text:
[Editor’s note: This review was originally published on September 6, 2026 at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release “ Possible Love ” in theaters on Friday, October 23 before it streams beginning on November 6.]

Another heart-stopping and novelistically layered stunner from modern cinema’s most literary auteur (a fiction author himself), Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love” might be dedicated to the memory of Krzysztof Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10,” but let’s dispel any notion of it being a remake. Conceived independently, and then lumped during pre-production into the same tribute omnibus that kicked off with Asghar Farhadi’s dreadful “ Parallel Tales ” at Cannes this year this film shares nothing in common with the final episode of Kieślowski’s series beyond the biblical commandment that Lee splays on screen at the very start: “Thou shalt not covet.”

And even then, the evidence of that instruction proves elusive in this sprawling drama about two very different couples who are brought together by the violent suppression of a workers’ strike at a major Korean metals factory. Who is coveting what, exactly?

It’s simple enough to understand what the film’s characters want on the surface — or at least that’s true of its women. A casually rich dilettante whose pale skin glows with the same lustrousness as her salon-perfect bob, first-time director Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong, similarly cast as the rich mom in “ Parasite ”) hopes to make a documentary about the declining state of labor across South Korea, with a particular focus on the recent unrest at a business called SP Heavy Industries. Although we see Ye-ji pitching the project to a grant board of some kind, the presumption is that most of her funding — and all of her creative freedom — has been provided by her imperiously chiseled husband Sang-woo (Lee newcomer Zo In-sung), a trust fund type who appears to enjoy a rather frictionless existence.

On the other side of the economic divide, the plucky but sad-eyed Mi-ok (played by “Secret Sunshine” actress Jeon Do-yeon, who delivers another once-a-century performance less than 20 years since her first collaboration with Lee) is clearly willing to do whatever it takes to bring her husband back to life. One of the “dead” who lost his job and sense of purpose in the mass layoffs at SP two years ago, her taciturn and implosive Ho-seok (“Peppermint Candy” star Sul Kyung-gu) has been a shell of himself since being injured amid the crackdown that ended the ensuing strike, and Mi-ok hopes that participating in Ye-ji’s doc might allow him to process his trauma — to stop shuffling around like a zombie and snap back into the man she once fell in love with as a teenage seamstress who didn’t have any better options. That he might become a more present father to their young son Cheol, whose current rudderlessness is best expressed by his abject incompetence at Taekwondo.

Beyond that simple baseline, the matrix of desire at work in Lee and Oh Jung-mi’s remarkably nuanced script is too slippery to pin down until the movie’s velvet gutpunch of a final scene. Yes, Mi-ok lusts after Ye-ji’s elegant wardrobe and designer handbags, and there’s an unspoken sexual charge in the air whenever she’s alone with Sang-woo (a charge that eventually sets fire to an unforgettable pre-dawn sequence on a private beach in the third act). But it would be unwisely reductive to conclude that the working-class woman is jealous of her hyper-affluent new bestie, just as it would be unhelpfully rash to assume that envy plays a more pivotal role in this story than resentment, or that a film as mottled and probing as “Possible Love” might be content to retrench the divide between Korea’s haves and have-nots.

Lee is perfectly happy to inflame our anger towards the one percent, and the movie’s jagged script — first inspired by a similar incident at a massive Korean company more than 10 years ago — is at its broadest when poking fun at how blithely Ye-ji inserts herself into Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s blue-collar world. She wants to be a fly on the wall in their downtrodden factory town, but the pampered documentarian stands out like a Maybach at a monastery; despite growing up without a silver spoon in her mouth, she rages at her inability to code-switch back to a lower rung on the financial ladder.

As the story goes on and Ye-ji convinces Mi-ok and Ho-seok to join them for a weekend at Sang-woo’s luxurious vacation house along the country’s western coast (all the better to entrap the couple on her turf where she can film them at all hours of the day), Lee finds a devious variety of ways to weaponize the running visual gag in which an intimate scene pans over to find Ye-ji hiding in the corner with her camera. It’s admirable that she wants to highlight how workers are being left behind as the ownership class automates their businesses in order to hoard their wealth, but Ye-ji fails to recognize the many condescending ways that she infringes upon her subjects’ dignity, as if — in a world where labor is increasingly rendered invisible from the people who profit from it — people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok should feel lucky to be seen at all.

In contrast to Lee’s monumental and more explosive “ Burning ,” the story he tells here builds on an instance of terrible violence rather than building to it, but his latest film simmers to a boil at a similar clip, and likewise alternates long dialogue scenes with indelible moments of visual acuity. While it’s hard for this comparatively restrained domestic saga to compete with Jeon Jong-seo’s sunset dance along the DMZ, Lee retains his gift for whipping spectacle out of thin air — for infusing something as routine as a car ride home or a quick dip in the ocean with an overwhelming degree of silent pathos. Every moment in “Possible Love” crackles like a wicked symphony of striated socioeconomic abrasion; every gesture, comment, and detail sharpens the strange geometry that brings these people closer together at the same time as it deepens the divides that will ultimately keep them apart.

Sometimes, in a handful of judiciously deployed moments, that geometry is expressed in skin-crawling fashion. Case in point: Sang-woo keeps an antique whistle on the living room mantle of his summer palace, and the resident “house fairy” — a seemingly non-verbal groundskeeper who Sang-woo used to play with when they were kids — is conditioned to come running whenever he blows on it. For the most part, however, the distance between the film’s characters is conveyed in subtler terms; in the confidence of Sang-woo’s upright posture, the brittleness of Mi-ok’s wavy hair, and the brusque impenetrability of Ho-seok’s blank stare, which doesn’t suggest the absence of an inner life so much as it betrays the constant struggle to bottle up his demons. He’s a prisoner of the pain that Ye-ji breezily documents like a tourist.

The careful attention that Lee pays to his characters’ bodies and how they wear them pays off — enormously — after “Possible Love” relocates to Sang-woo’s summer home for this 164-minute film’s last hour (“This is like a house from a novel I haven’t read,” Mi-ok gawps over dinner). Between a night of drunken karaoke and a few pre-dawn strolls along the mansion’s private beach, the movie’s financially driven exploration of freedom and power begin to assume a more physical dimension, a transition which threatens to confuse the dynamics that have otherwise tethered everyone to their roles; this is where Jeon seizes control, her raw and marbled performance reaching a state of self-preservation so primal that it renders the rest of the characters senseless.

“Possible Love” takes brilliant — if unnerving — pleasure in leveling the playing field between its two couples, but those shifty indulgences are too freighted with reality to feel like wish fulfillment. The film isn’t naive enough to pretend that its “poor” characters might ever achieve true equilibrium with its rich ones, nor is it patronizing enough to suggest that there’s some kind of implicit dignity to being exploited by the carelessness of late capitalism. Ho-seok is not a holy sufferer, he’s a profoundly broken and embittered man whose plight speaks to the hopelessness of fighting back against a system that’s designed to trample people like him, and Lee is far more interested in rendering his pain than he is in “solving” it.

The ultimate power of “Possible Love,” which grows in the mind after it’s over (and greatly rewards any repeat viewings), is rooted in neither wanton despair nor false optimism. Despite being steeped in the sadness and frustration of the working class, Lee’s drama uses its film-within-a-film construct to refract the moral valences of labor through the prism of what people actually earn through their work.

Slumming it as a documentarian as she builds towards her dream of being a narrative filmmaker (“Imagining things is my hobby” is maybe not what you want to hear from the person directing a documentary about your life), Ye-ji is a victim of her own second-hand affluence — the seamlessness of her life has life has made it so that she has to performatively “method act” in order to get close to her subjects and shoot anything real. Her observational technique is a parody of the invisible labor that she laments noticing the first time during a trip to a luxurious Qattari hotel, but she can’t even see people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok unless she contrives a scenario for them to exist for her camera.

For his part, Sang-woo’s work is so frictionless that he can buy and sell entire companies from his laptop while sipping a latte, and his marriage to Ye-ji feels like it’s laminated in plastic. They passively snipe at each other in short bursts so as not to get any dirt on the bedsheets, and relegate all of their latent desires to the blind spots that rich people create so that they don’t have to see the world beyond their own wealth.

By contrast, Mi-ok and Ho-seok have no choice but to confront the hardships that have been visited upon them, and to want for things so badly they can never lose sight of the work they’ve put into each other. Their lives are principled upon a possible love, because they don’t have the luxury of pretending there’s any other kind. Yes, their history together — fleshed out in a series of perfectly modulated flashbacks — is clumsy and imperfect, and their financial prospects for the future are tenuous at best, but they will never have to covet what this world still offers to people for free. Mi-ok and Ho-seok have always felt as if the moon shined only for them at night, and the final moments of this gently shattering and astonishingly well-shaded drama exalt in the freedom they give to each other by saving its glow for themselves.

Grade: A

“Possible Love” premiered at the 2026 Venice Film Festival. Netflix will release it in theaters on Friday, October 23, and on Netflix on Friday, November 6.
excerpt_original: Class conflict achieves vivid new dimension in this sprawling Netflix drama about the relationship between a rich documentary filmmaker and her blue collar subjects.

article_text:
メールマガジン登録者のメールアドレス漏えいに関するお詫びとお知らせ

平素より当メディアをご利用いただき、誠にありがとうございます。

このたび、当メディアがメールマガジンの配信に利用している外部サービス「ブラストメール」（株式会社ラクスライトクラウド運営）が第三者による不正アクセスを受け、当メディアのメールマガジン「Newsletter」の配信にご登録いただいている皆さまのメールアドレスが外部に漏えいしたことが判明いたしました。

皆さまに多大なるご心配とご迷惑をおかけしますことを、心よりお詫び申し上げます。

本事案の概要は以下のとおりです。

■ 発覚の経緯と原因

2026年10月21日、メール配信サービス「ブラストメール」の運営会社より、第三者による不正アクセスが発生したとの報告を受けました。

その後、同社による漏えい情報の調査が進められ、10月23日朝、当メディアのメールマガジン登録者のメールアドレスが漏えいしたことが確認され、同社より報告を受けました。

同社の調査によると、外部の第三者がAPI用サーバーに侵入し、サービスのデータベースなどにアクセスして情報を持ち出したことが確認されています。詳しい侵入経路については、現在も調査が続けられています。

■ 漏えいした個人データ

当メディアのメールマガジン登録者全員のメールアドレスです。

当メディアでは、メールマガジンの登録に際して氏名や住所などの個人情報は取得しておらず、今回漏えいした登録者情報はメールアドレスのみとなります。

■ 当社の対応

現在、ブラストメールの運営会社において、原因の究明および再発防止に向けた調査が進められています。当社においても、同社と連携し、必要な対応を進めてまいります。

また、本件については、個人情報保護委員会への報告手続きを進めております。

なお、現在ブラストメールの配信サービスが停止しているため、メールマガジン登録者の皆さまへのメールによる個別のお知らせができない状況です。このため、まずは当メディア上でご報告しております。

当面、メールマガジンの配信は一時停止させていただきます。配信再開のめどが立ち次第、当メディア上でお知らせいたします。今後、新たな事実が判明した場合には、必要に応じてご報告いたします。

本件に関しまして、皆さまにご心配とご迷惑をおかけしておりますことを、重ねて深くお詫び申し上げます。

article_text:
The Alexandria-born, Athens-based artist explains how her emotions influence the background colours of her urban and natural landscape paintings.

Canvas: How would you describe your paintings to someone who has not yet experienced them?

Farida El Gazzar: There is very much an element of conformity to my grid. I don’t use rulers, so there’s always a little bit of a twist to that rigidity, a humorous element I want to put in the architecture, but there’s also the contradiction of architecture that’s depicted in this way. When you’re in a wild natural space, such as a field of plants, it creates a sort of free-form architecture. I’m interested in forms and shapes, so I juxtapose these two elements, the rigid against the free-flowing. The two are usually connected by a vibrant or uniform background, because I’m also interested in bringing out the subject and making it more monumental.

Nature is an ongoing inspiration. I might pass the same object many times, but with each encounter, something has changed. I like that evolution or zooming in just to capture something, like a detail.

Does that have to do with the colours you use, reflecting the evolution through the seasons?

Subconsciously, yes. I think that when I’m painting, depending on where I am and what time of the year it is, the colours that I choose and the way I’m painting have a different feel. That’s why I usually know around what time or what period I was working on these paintings. They tend to have something subtle in common. But again, when I combine them with another group of paintings I have done before, they start to create a new dialogue.

Were Together Tangled and Red Moon Blossom created around the same time? They both feature lone trees centred on a deep blue or red background.

Those two works were created for an exhibition called Night Garden in 2019 at Kalfayan Galleries in Athens. The paintings are between the metaphysical, the subconscious and the dream, alluding to that trance-like state you can go into when in nature. At that time, especially, I felt like I needed to dive into my painting as a form of meditation. Looking back at those pieces, I realise that they’re a bit darker than my more recent ones. I like the element of bringing light within darkness, so I try to enhance that aspect, especially in that series of works.

Do you have an idea of the background colours before you start to paint?

I don’t like to fixate on a set idea before I paint because there’s always another energy when there is a sense of flow. I usually have an idea, but I don’t stick to it necessarily. It’s always a work in progress. If I don’t like something, I just add a layer on top.

I am often inspired by what is around me. My favourite time of day is sunset, because it creates a sort of stillness, a pause. In Athens, where I live, the light is great, so that also inspires me. For example, in Neighbours (2015) you can see the colours of the setting sun behind an apartment block. The quality of the sunset can vary so much, depending on the place. I find that in Egypt, the light is a little bit more orange, a bit more golden.I like to play with those colours.

How do you compose your images?

I take a lot of pictures and use them as my resources, mixing and matching them, creating snapshots to capture a moment. I also take photographs while travelling, as that is when we see things objectively, with a clear mind. So I pick up on these little characteristics of a place, but again, there aren’t any people in my works. The energy of human presence is felt, not seen, through the creation of structures, the way the landscape has been formed, or the remains of what has been left behind.

Sometimes that human presence feels more overt, such as in Untitled (15) (2011), which depicts the vitrine of a shoe shop.

That was from a series of paintings called Alexandrian Vitrines . It started when I was in Alexandria, where my family is from. This particular shoe shop is in the downtown area, in the alleyways where there were traditional shops, including jewellery shops, tailors, hatmakers and antique sellers. The way the vitrines were displayed felt very timeless, as though they could have been from 60 years ago, but nothing had changed. There was a certain kind of safety and security that I felt from that. I also found the way the jewellery was generously displayed in the vitrines of the shops, shown for everybody to see, very beautiful. This generosity, and the gold, made me feel very happy as I was walking around. There was a sense of energy and euphoria there.

What does colour mean to you? What can it convey that lines cannot?

Although many times I think of painting in black and white, which I like for that interesting use of greyscale tones, colour is a strong element of expression in my work because it always enhances an emotion.

This interview first appeared in Canvas 124: Prismatic

article_text:
「美」を「見る」とはどういうことか。ポーラ「B.A」がTokyo Gendaiでひらいた新たな視点

江戸時代の浮世絵と鏡台、東信のアートワーク、そして現代アートの見方をひらくガイドツアー。 Tokyo Gendai 2026にオフィシャル・ビューティー・パートナーとして参加した ポーラ B.Aが、アートフェアという場を通じて提示した「美」と「見ること」の可能性をレポートする。

2026年9月に横浜で開催された国際アートフェア「 Tokyo Gendai 」で、会期を通じてひときわ賑わっている一角があった。同イベントにオフィシャル・ビューティー・パートナーとして参加した、 ポーラ の最高峰ブランド「B.A」のブースだ。

太古の自然から植物、そして人間の気配へ──異なる時間軸に属するものを作品の中に重ねることで「時間とは何か」を考えさせる、フラワーアーティストの東信による象徴的なアートワークが、ブースの入り口で来場者を迎え入れる。長年コラボレーションを続けるB.Aと東に共通するのは、固定された「美」ではなく、変化し続ける生命そのものに美を見出そうとする視点だ。

ブランドが「Inclusion Black」と呼ぶ黒を基調としたその空間に足を踏み入れると、まず、江戸時代後期の浮世絵に目が奪われる。展示されたのは、化粧文化を学術的に研究するポーラ文化研究所が所蔵する《江戸名所百人美女》から選ばれた4点のレプリカ。同研究所では、国内外の化粧道具や装身具、文献、浮世絵などの歴史資料を収集し、時代によって移り変わる美容や化粧の文化を研究してきた。

《江戸名所百人美女》には、江戸の名所とともに、その土地にゆかりのある女性たちの日常が描かれている。今回紹介された作品にも、櫛で髪をとかす、湯で顔をぬぐう、眉を整える、鏡で首元を確かめるといった仕草が登場する。その傍らには、作品の中にも描かれている江戸時代後期の鏡台が置かれ、紅や白粉、刷毛といった当時の化粧道具も展示された。

鏡を見る。肌を整える。髪を整える。そしてもう一度、自分の姿を確かめる。江戸時代に鏡の普及が進み、鏡台が一部の特権階級だけではなく裕福な町人にも広がっていったことを考えれば、鏡の前で自分自身を見つめる時間そのものが、人々の日常へと入り込んでいった時代だったことが窺える。

人の身体から生まれたB.Aのかたち

その数百年後に位置するものとして展示されていたのが、1985年に誕生し、41年目を迎えたB.Aだ。昨秋、第7世代へとリニューアルしたB.Aのボトルには直線がなく、人間の身体を思わせる曲線によって構成されている。そのため、見る角度によって輪郭や表情が変化する。社内デザイナーが人体のスケッチを繰り返し、人の造形美と向き合うことから生まれたデザインには、B.Aが掲げる「人の可能性は広がる」という考え方の通り、その人の中に存在する可能性をどう引き出すかというブランドの思想が反映されている。そして、「美」とは完成された一つの理想像に近づくことではないというメッセージも受け取ることができる。

ブースにはさらに、プリツカー賞建築家であり、世界各地の美術館建築でも知られるSANAAの妹島和世が空間設計を手がけたポーラのグローバルフラッグシップストア、ポーラ ギンザの模型も展示された。

アートフェアの「舞台裏」

そして今回、ブース展示と並んでもう一つの重要な取り組みとなったのが、Tokyo Gendaiの会場を巡るスペシャルガイドツアーだ。

会期を通じてTokyo GendaiのVIP、ポーラの顧客、ARTnews JAPANの読者など、約73人が参加した。Tokyo Gendaiを含むアートフェアそのものを訪れるのが初めてという人が半数以上を占めた一方、海外の美術館を訪ねたり、国内の展覧会に足を運んだり、美大で制作を学んでいたりと、それぞれに異なるかたちでアートと接点を持つ人が多かった。

ツアーが目指したのは、注目作品を順番に紹介する、いわゆる「見どころツアー」とは少し異なるものだった。ガイドは参加者の関心や当日の会場の状況に応じてルートを変えながら、個々の作品や作家だけでなく、そもそもアートフェアとはどのような場所なのか、ギャラリーはどんな役割を果たし、作品の評価や流通はどのように形づくられていくのか、といった背景にも話を広げた。

ガイドの一人、キュレーターの三宅敦大は、作品の解説以上に「フェアという場所の特性や意義、多様性」を伝えることを意識したという。フェアの構造を俯瞰することは、ギャラリーの立場やアーティストの社会的評価を理解し、自分自身で作品の背景や文脈を探っていく手がかりになるからだ。実際、作品についてあえて説明しすぎないことで、参加者同士が自分の気になった作品を紹介し合う場面も生まれたという。

教える人と教えられる人に分かれるのではなく、それぞれの「見る」が交換されていく。それは、アートフェアを別の角度から体験する方法でもあった。

見る人自身の「視点」をひらく

参加者の反応が大きかったのも、必ずしも有名作家の作品解説だけではなかった。たとえばHaruka Ito by Islandのブースでは、谷口正造の作品を目当てにVIPプレビューの入場列に並んだコレクターが複数いたことや、作品が早々に売約となったエピソードを紹介。参加者は、作品そのものだけでなく、作家を支えるギャラリーとコレクター、そして市場の関係にも強い関心を示した。別の回では、参加者が会場に居合わせたライアン・ガンダーと10分ほど言葉を交わす場面もあった。

現代美術を理解するためには、必ずしも美術史の知識から入る必要はない。自分がすでに持っている経験や知識を足場にして、目の前の作品や、それを取り巻く世界へ入っていくこともできる。ガイドを務めた半田颯哉がツアーで意識したのも、参加者が後日、別の展覧会で知らない作家の作品に出会ったときにも楽しめるような「視点」を持ち帰ってもらうことだった。

普段なら「わからない」と通り過ぎてしまうかもしれない作品の前で立ち止まり、見る。疑問があれば質問し、自分なりに考え、誰かと感想を交わしてみる。こうした体験もまた、多くの作品と、それをつくり、売り、買い、見る人々が一つの場所に集まるアートフェアならではの醍醐味であり、そこでのコミュニケーションを通じて、ひいては作品を所有するという選択肢を考える最初の一歩にもなり得る。

こうして振り返ると、Tokyo Gendaiで展開された、江戸時代の浮世絵や鏡台、B.A、東信のアートワーク、そしてガイドツアーという一見異なる試みに、一つの共通項が見えてくる。

それは、何を美しいとするかを一方的に提示するのではなく、見る人自身の視点をひらくことだ。江戸時代の女性が鏡台の前で自分の姿を見つめる。現代の私たちが鏡の前で自分の肌に触れる。そしてアートフェアで、これまで知らなかった作品の前に立ち止まる。そこで行われているのは、すでに知っている「美」を確認することだけではない。これまで見えていなかった何かを見つけること。そして、自分自身の見方が変わる可能性に出会うことなのかもしれない。

title_original: Azu Nwagbogu to Helm Tasweer Photography Biennial 2027
editorial_title_zh: 阿祖·恩瓦博古将担任 2027 年塔斯维尔摄影双年展艺术总监

article_text:
News

Azu Nwagbogu to Helm Tasweer Photography Biennial 2027

AZU NWAGBOGU . Photo by Anastasia Ermolenko. Courtesy the Tasweer Photography Biennial.

Qatar Museums (QM) has appointed Nigerian curator Azu Nwagbogu as the artistic director of the fourth Tasweer Photography Biennial, slated to open in Doha in April 2027.

Nwagbogu brings nearly two decades of leadership experience to the role. He is the founder and director of the nonprofit African Artists’ Foundation (AAF) in Lagos, and established the LagosPhoto Festival in 2010, marking Nigeria’s first international exhibition dedicated to photography. His curatorial practice centers on marginalized histories, interrogating Western-centric narratives while exploring questions of repatriation and decolonial identity. In 2017, Nwagbogu joined the Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa (Zeitz MOCAA) in Cape Town as curator at large of photography, later serving as the institution’s interim director and chief curator from 2018 to 2019.

Beyond curating shows at AAF and Zeitz MOCAA, Nwagbogu has overseen projects at various institutions across the globe, from the Centre for Fine Arts in Brussels and the Rencontres d’Arles to the Savannah Centre for Contemporary Art in Tamale. In 2024, he led Benin’s inaugural pavilion at the 60th Venice Biennale, which featured four artists examining spirituality, Pan-Africanism, and ecological fragility. He is also the recipient of the Royal Photographic Society’s 2021 Curator of the Year Award and was named a 2026 Art Basel Medalist in the Curator category.

In a press release, Nwagbogu expressed his gratitude over the appointment, noting, “Images have always shaped our perception of the world; what is new is the speed and scale of their circulation, and the new ways they ask us to look, remember, and interpret. Tasweer creates an important space to engage and host that changing visual language with ethical and intellectual courage.”

Launched by QM in 2021 under the auspices of QM chairperson Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, Tasweer is a leading platform for emerging and established lens-based practitioners from West Asia and beyond. The 2027 edition is the first to be presented under QM’s forthcoming Art Mill Museum.

Eva Brank is an editorial intern at ArtAsiaPacific.
excerpt_original: The Nigerian curator will direct the fourth edition, slated to open in Doha in April 2027. Eva Brank

editorial_title_zh: 一本打开的书：如何拍出伟大的电影改编作品，从《闪灵》到《猜火车》
editorial_excerpt_zh: 并非每一部伟大的小说都能拍出伟大的电影，反之亦然。但无论源文本如何，或者那些备受喜爱的角色如何被对待，通往成功改编的途径不止一条。追赶流行总是很有趣，就像一个维多利亚时代的人对高轮自行车疯狂着迷……

"追赶流行总是很有趣，就像一个维多利亚时代的人对高轮自行车疯狂着迷。这大概就是为什么，违背我更好的判断，我今年夏天去看了克里斯托弗·诺兰的大片《奥德赛》，和大家一起买票加入了这场大众对话。今年另一部引发争议的改编作品是埃默拉尔德·芬尼尔的《呼啸山庄》，还没等观众看这部电影，全世界就都在和他的妻子争论不休。毫无疑问，最近那部《理智与情感》电影的制作方也希望很多人能去看，看看他们是否会讨厌它。", {"type": "paragraph", "text": "毕竟，我们很少有人在离开电影院时会说：“这跟我脑子里想象的一模一样。”或者更不可能说：“这比书还要好。”我们更有可能会挥舞拳头，抱怨他们是怎么毁了结局、把内容拍得降智、不可饶恕地选了一个头发不对的演员，或者背叛了一个深受喜爱的角色，就像去年的“谋杀俱乐部周四”惨剧那样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/1c94399a471a65b92467034f67a60d4242193278/0_0_3469_2452/master/3469.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "《猜火车》。", "caption": "全员登船……《猜火车》。摄影：AJ Pics/Alamy", "首先要说的是，源文本的质量并不重要。我在进行研究时抱有一些相当固定的想法：例如，安东尼·伯吉斯所写的，“优秀的改编几乎总是取材于二流或三流小说”；有些作品是“无法拍成电影的”；经典作品在电视上有更多“呼吸的空间”。不久我便意识到这些全都不对。是的，有时平庸的小说——例如60年代末和70年代初的三巨头《大白鲨》、《教父》和《驱魔人》——在银幕上可以被调校到天才的水平。但伟大的书也能拍出伟大的电影：《猜火车》、《送信人》、《豹》以及伯吉斯自己的《发条橙》只是其中的几个例子。有时，就像《达芬奇密码》和《五十度灰》那样，一本极度愚蠢的书也会拍成一部极度愚蠢的电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "诚然，某些书籍确实更容易被搬上银幕。简·奥斯汀那些无懈可击的受阻爱情情节是模版，可以披上任何时代的外衣，就像雪儿·霍洛维茨在《独领风骚》开场时用来规划服装的电脑模板一样——那是自由发挥改编的极致。奥斯汀的小说包含了所有浪漫喜剧的DNA，正如《鲁滨逊漂流记》存在于《火星救援》中，哥特小说存在于恐怖电影中，或者《圣诞颂歌》存在于每一部圣诞电影中。短篇小说带着曲折的惊悚感和直奔结局的冲动，似乎天生就是为电影打造的；我最喜欢的电影《现在别看》就是改编自达夫妮·杜穆里耶的中篇小说。神话及其近亲民间故事和童话故事扑朔迷离的起源与弹性，使它们能够被无休止地改编，因为它们留下了空白，让电影人能够用自己的想象力去填补。", "links": [{"text": "Jane Austen", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/books/gallery/2017/jul/18/jane-austens-facts-and-figures-in-charts"}, {"text": "Don’t Look Now", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/2023/oct/16/dont-look-now-nicolas-roeg-donald-sutherland-julie-christie"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "不忠实通常很有帮助。一些最好的改编作品与源材料调情，采取可怕的自由发挥，然后像小报里的负心汉一样抛弃它。“偷走你需要的零件，然后以你能跑的最快速度逃跑，”保罗·托马斯·安德森曾建议；希区柯克声称他在拍自己的版本之前只读了一次《群鸟》，之后就再也没想过它。（我曾交谈过的一位编剧告诉我，他曾被要求不要去读他正在改编的小说，因为制作公司认为这会成为一种阻碍。）书籍和电影是完全不同的野兽，正如作家兼编剧丹尼斯·勒hane曾说过的，“苹果与长颈鹿”。改编是从言语到视觉的翻译。电影人需要找到他们自己的语言。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/aa0866c852b264d6f8cd842d7fe0854938c523a7/140_0_2450_1960/master/2450.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "《人类之子》。", "caption": "宝贝，你已经走过了漫长的道路……《人类之子》。摄影：AJ Pics/Alamy", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我最深爱的非忠实改编作品之一是阿方索·卡隆2006年的《人类之子》，不仅因为它由处于身体完美巅峰状态的克里夫·欧文主演。它成功地将保守党贵族P·D·詹姆斯那部理性的、神学性的小说，转化成了一部关于民粹主义、恐怖以及我们如何对待移民的反乌托邦惊悚片，这部作品——尽管如今已有二十年历史——却显得一年比一年新鲜。（詹姆斯对此感到非常高兴。）卡隆将小说作为跳板，然后将其抛在脑后，去追寻他自己的冒险。留下来的是核心概念：如果我们生活在一个没有孩子的世界里会怎样？科幻小说和推想小说的“如果会怎样”的高概念非常适合随心所欲地发挥：它是一个容器，电影人可以将自己的关注点以及他们那个时代的焦虑倾注其中。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当编剧兼导演萨利·波特（Sally Potter）重塑弗吉尼亚·伍尔夫（Virginia Woolf）的穿越时空奇幻小说《奥兰多》时，她对待它的方式“就好像这本书从未存在过”，将其变成了一记对刚刚通过第28条（section 28）的英国建制派的豪华嘲讽。她说，她对这部小说残酷一点，是为了对电影好一点。这就是毁灭即创造的信条。在合适的编剧和导演手中，原著可以而且应当听从他们的意志：斯坦利·库布里克（Stanley Kubrick）背叛了斯蒂芬·金（Stephen King）对《闪灵》的构想，却打造了一部大师之作。《黑暗的心》蜕变成了战争史诗《现代启示录》；《红龙》则变成了——嗯，一部迈克尔·曼（Michael Mann）风格的电影，那部催眠般的《猎人者》。一部改编作品绝不应该是一张空洞的金曲精选辑。对文学原著过于敬畏可能会毁了它，这就是为什么我猜测诸如《饥饿游戏》和《长路》这样制作精美、充满风格且几无改动的电影，对我而言在银幕上显得略微缺乏血色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "话说回来，任何东西真的能做到忠实吗，又忠实于什么呢？没有哪个故事是100%原创的。（正如《异形》编剧丹·奥班农所说：“我没有抄袭任何人。我抄袭了所有人！”）我甚至不认为你能做到“忠于文本的精神”，因为对于每个人来说，精神都是不一样的。我们在阅读时，脑海里都在播放各自的小电影。许多人将《了不起的盖茨比》视为美国的丧钟；而改编者往往会想：“派对！”我认为希思克利夫是个喜欢吊死小狗的精神病患者；但后来的历任导演显然不这么认为。我很高兴发现茱迪·福斯特（Jodie Foster）曾极力争取在《沉默的羔羊》中饰演克拉丽丝·史达琳（Clarice Starling），因为在她看来，这部小说讲述的是一个女人在“所有这些该死的男人”从中作梗的同时，拯救另一个女人生命的故事。改编作品或许只是窥探另一个心灵世界的一瞥，但他们的画面却很少能与我们想象的一致。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "这方面最明显的例子或许就是选角。正如黑夜紧随白昼一样，好莱坞挑选的演员往往比严格需要的好看，尽管还不至于达到《黑日危机》中丹妮丝·理查兹（Denise Richards）穿着热裤扮演核物理学家的地步。这可能是刻意的：在罗伯特·布洛克（Robert Bloch）的小说《惊魂记》中，诺曼·贝茨（Norman Bates）在外表上令人反感；而希区柯克希望由面相甜美的安东尼·博金斯（Anthony article_text:
I t is always fun to join in a craze, like a Victorian going mad for penny farthings. Which is probably why, against my better judgment, I went to see Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey this summer, buying my ticket into the popular conversation along with everyone else. This year’s other divisive adaptation, Emerald Fennell’s Wuthering Heights, had the world and his wife arguing about it before they had even watched the film. No doubt the makers of the recent Sense and Sensibility movie were also hoping for lots of people to go and see it to discover whether they hated it.

After all, very few of us leave the cinema saying: “That’s exactly how I pictured it in my head.” Or even less likely: “That was better than the book.” We’re more likely to shake our fists at how they ruined the ending, dumbed it down, unforgivably cast somebody with the wrong hair, or betrayed a beloved character, as with last year’s Thursday Murder Club debacle.

But what makes a good adaptation? Like Odysseus himself, and as every Nancy Meyers fan knows: it’s complicated. I have just written a book about the towering heights and profane depths of adaptation, The Book Was Better, for which I subjected myself to some of the worst viewing experiences possible, including the soft rock opera musical Heathcliff; 1996’s freakishly bad The Island of Dr Moreau; and a horrible three-part version of Ayn Rand’s Atlas Shrugged. But I also saw plenty of masterpieces that equalled or sometimes surpassed the originals. Here’s what I learned.

The first thing to say is that the quality of the source is irrelevant. I went into my research with some pretty fixed ideas: for instance, that “the brilliant adaptations are nearly always of fiction of the second or third class”, as Anthony Burgess wrote; that some works are “unfilmable”; that classics have more “room to breathe” on TV. Soon I realised none of these were true. Yes, sometimes workmanlike novels, such as the late 60s and early 70s triumvirate Jaws, The Godfather and The Exorcist, can be tuned to a level of genius on screen. But great books can make great films, too: Trainspotting, The Go-Between, The Leopard and Burgess’s own A Clockwork Orange are just a few examples. And sometimes, in the case of The Da Vinci Code and Fifty Shades of Grey, a deeply silly book becomes a deeply silly film.

It is true that certain books lend themselves to the screen more readily. Jane Austen ’s immaculate plots of love impeded are templates that can be dressed up in the clothes of any age, like the computer template Cher Horowitz uses to plan her outfits at the start of Clueless – the ne plus ultra of free-handed adaptations. Austen’s novels contain the DNA of all romcoms, just as Robinson Crusoe is found in The Martian, the gothic novel in horror films, or A Christmas Carol in every single Christmas movie. Short stories, with their twisty shocks and rush towards the end point, seem made for cinema; my favourite film, Don’t Look Now , is based on a Daphne du Maurier novella. The murky origins and elasticity of myths and their close cousins, folk and fairytales, make them ceaselessly adaptable, because they leave gaps for a film-maker to fill with their own imaginations.

Being unfaithful is usually helpful. Some of the best adaptations flirt with the source material, taking frightful liberties and then abandoning it like a tabloid love rat. “Steal the parts that you need, and then run as fast as you can,” advised Paul Thomas Anderson; Hitchcock claimed he read The Birds once before making his version, and never thought about it again. (One screenwriter I spoke to told me he was once asked not to read the novel he was adapting as the production company thought it would be a hindrance). Books and films are entirely different beasts, “apples and giraffes”, as author-screenwriter Dennis Lehane once said. Adaptation is an act of translation from the verbal to the visual. A film-maker needs to find their own language.

One of my most beloved unfaithful adaptations is Alfonso Cuarón’s 2006 Children of Men, and not just because it stars Clive Owen at the peak of his physical perfection. It manages to transform a cerebral, theological novel by the Conservative peer PD James into a dystopian thriller about populism, terror and how we treat immigrants, one which – although now two decades old – feels fresher each year. (James was delighted with it.) Cuarón used the novel as a jumping-off point, then left it behind to follow his own adventure. What remained was the central conceit: what if we lived in a world without children? The “what if” high concepts of science fiction and speculative fiction are perfect for playing fast and loose with: a vessel into which a film-maker’s own preoccupations, and the anxieties of their age, can be poured.

When writer-director Sally Potter reinvented Virginia Woolf’s time-travelling fantasia Orlando, she treated it “as if the book never existed”, turning it into a lavish nose-thumb to a UK establishment that had just passed section 28. She was, she said, cruel to the novel to be kind to the film. It’s the destruction-as-creation mantra. In the hands of the right writer and director, a source can, and should, be made to submit to their will: Stanley Kubrick betrayed Stephen King’s vision of The Shining but made a tour de force. Heart of Darkness mutated into a war epic with Apocalypse Now; Red Dragon became, well, a Michael Mann film, the hypnotic Manhunter. An adaptation should never be a hollow greatest hits album. Being too reverential towards a literary source can kill it, which is why I suspect films such as The Hunger Games and The Road, lovingly and stylishly made with few changes, felt slightly bloodless on screen to me.

Can anything really be faithful anyway, and to what? No story is 100 per cent original. (As Alien screenwriter Dan O’Bannon said: “I didn’t steal from anybody. I stole from everybody !”) I don’t even think you can be “true to the spirit” of a text, because the spirit is different for everyone. We all have our own little films running in our heads when we read. Many see The Great Gatsby as a death knell for the US; adapters tend to think: “parties!”. I think Heathcliff is a psychopath who likes to hang little dogs; successive directors clearly didn’t. I loved discovering that Jodie Foster lobbied hard for the part of Clarice Starling in The Silence of the Lambs because, for her, the novel was about a woman saving the life of another woman while “all these fucking men” get in the way. An adaptation may just be a glimpse into another mind’s eye, but their pictures seldom match the ones we had imagined.

Perhaps the most obvious example of this is casting. As sure as night follows day, Hollywood casts a better-looking actor than strictly necessary, although not always reaching “Denise Richards in hotpants as a nuclear physicist in The World is Not Enough” levels. This can be deliberate: in Robert Bloch’s novel Psycho, Norman Bates is physically repellent; Hitchcock wanted the sweet-faced Anthony Perkins for the part to wrongfoot the audience. More often it’s because, as the critic Roger Ebert observed, cinema is a machine for generating empathy, so the thinking goes that leads should be “likable” – which backfired horribly when Bruce Willis was cast as a desiccated English journalist in the notoriously disastrous adaptation of Tom Wolfe’s The Bonfire of the Vanities. But sometimes an actor who is wrong on paper can make a role their own, whether it’s Margaret Rutherford as Miss Marple, Renée Zellweger as Bridget Jones or Michael Caine as Harry Palmer in The Ipcress File (in Len Deighton’s novels he’s a northerner and doesn’t have a name). Charisma goes a long way.

Perhaps in the end, adaptation all comes down to emotions and sensations. “You’ve drunk the drink, and the taste that’s left in your mouth is what you go with,” as Anthony Minghella described adapting The Talented Mr Ripley. Irvine Welsh said you must smell the books. Hossein Amini, who reinvented The Wings of the Dove as “noir in costume”, wanted to recapture that ecstatic moment when “nobody else in the world understood or experienced that book exactly like I did”.

Returning to The Odyssey, I wonder why, even though Nolan did the right things, subordinating it to his worldview and faithlessly reinventing it for our age by turning a wily trickster into a traumatised veteran, the film just made me feel as if I’d been in a war: long periods of boredom and waiting punctuated by violence. Perhaps, ultimately, he overthought it and should have felt it instead? Or maybe, as the late Hilary Mantel said of adaptation, you must “put down the text, and dream it”.

The Book Was Better by Louise Willder (Oneworld, £14.99). To order a copy for £13.49 go to guardianbookshop.com Delivery charges may apply.

article_text:
The exhibition functions as a window into a neglected area of Cuban art. It makes it possible to recognize interconnected artistic trajectories, lives, and aspirations that would otherwise appear as isolated and unique. Explorations of identity, memory, and the body emerge as ways of reclaiming imagined origins and participation in an existential and symbolic heritage fractured by forced diaspora. [v]

Counter-Visualities and Resistance in the Exhibition My Own Past : A Maroon Genealogy of Afrodescendant Cuban Art

From the galleries of the Lowe Art Museum in Miami, the exhibition My Own Past: Afrodescendant Contributions to Cuban Art , opened its doors in May to restore the cartography of Afrodescendant Cuban art—the aesthetic production of a population group that has been structurally subordinated and constituted as Cuba’s social “other.” Through art, Afrodescendant creators have become agents in constructing their own narratives and imaginaries, giving rise to narratives and strategies of resistance that this exhibition seeks to recover. The exhibition is a new, expanded iteration of a previous version shown at the Ethelbert Cooper Gallery of African & African American Art at Harvard University in 2022. Organized and curated by Alejandro de la Fuente, director of the Afro-Latin American Research Institute at Harvard, in collaboration with Bárbaro Martínez-Ruiz and Cary A. García Yero, the exhibition represents an ethical gesture of recovery and repair for historically marginalized practices. [i] It also calls attention to the systemic inequities that Cubans racialized as negros continue to endure amid the country’s ongoing social crisis.

The expressive depth and originality of the figurative languages developed by peripheral and counter-hegemonic subjects are revitalized through the collection of works now on view in Miami. Alongside nineteenth-century, avant-garde, and contemporary works of immense artistic and cultural value, the exhibition’s poetic movements allow visitors to appreciate, up close, the human and creative efforts of artists who succeeded in transgressing the logics of segregation and the racialization of labor through artistic practice.

In the works that comprise My Own Past , every painterly tone and sculptural relief can be understood as a subversion of the “instrumentality of Black life and labor.” [ii] Technical mastery emerges as a triumph—a form of struggle against exclusion and subordination, the mechanism of colonial domination identified by Nelson Maldonado-Torres. [iii] Artistic practice by non-white bodies crystallized as a means of emancipating their intellectual, expressive, and physical capacities from the racial order that confined them to necessity and exploitation. [iv]

The exhibition offers a historical reconstruction of the aesthetic trajectories of those sectors in Cuba that were dispossessed of rights and agency. Its curatorial narrative unfolds through rigorous research that illuminates both social contexts and art-historical questions. As a multidisciplinary project, it creates an immersive experience that brings together not only artworks but also documents and historical archives. A whole section of the exhibition is devoted to documentary materials. It reconnects the fragments of a previously mutilated narrative, vindicating artistic practices that have long been marginalized and ignored.

The exhibition functions as a window into a neglected area of Cuban art. It makes it possible to recognize interconnected artistic trajectories, lives, and aspirations that would otherwise appear as isolated and unique. Explorations of identity, memory, and the body emerge as ways of reclaiming imagined origins and participation in an existential and symbolic heritage fractured by forced diaspora. [v]

The exhibition also invites viewers to admire, within these hybrid archipelagic figurations, a sensorium in which symbols rooted in African traditions intersect with artistic languages from across the Atlantic, including those of Europe. These narratives of reinvention transformed the fragments of a denied culture into a rich, densely layered sensibility. Art became a means of sustaining spiritual traditions, cultural practices, and foundational genealogies.

As visitors move through the exhibition, they encounter the role of art in recovering neglected temporalities and affective histories. Participation in an unnamed tradition gives rise to what might be called a maroon genealogy—the restoration of a lineage and artistic tradition that Black artists renew through their work. This amounts to reclaiming a visual inheritance, as exemplified by Elio Rodríguez’s revival and commentary on The Jungle by Wifredo Lam. It is a tribute to the iconic Afro-Caribbean artist, but Elio injects new textures and sensual dimensions into Lam’s work while reconfiguring its exuberant rhythms through a contemporary visual language.

The worlds and lives excluded from official artistic representations gradually take shape through this body of work, through this unique constellation of artists and their creations. These artists challenge asymmetries of power, oppression, and social inequality—themes that the exhibition forcefully brings to the foreground. The works in My Own Past emerge as counter-visualities: visual expressions of what has been previously excluded, critical sites that convey the tensions experienced by bodies and subjects marked as “other.”

Identifying and reconnecting the fragments of this once-silenced narrative is one of the exhibition’s greatest achievements. Through aesthetic practice, Afrodescendant Cuban artists have developed their own imaginaries, enacted political interventions, and contributed to the construction of collective identities. My Own Past gathers these artistic trajectories as acts of recognition, memory, and presence.

Afrocubanismo: Highlights from the Ramón and Nercys Cernuda Collection , an exhibition dedicated to exploring how the avant-garde movements of the 1930s and 1940s reimagined Cuba through Afro-Cuban culture, is presented in the adjacent galleries of the Lowe Art Museum. Unlike My Own Past , the artists featured in Afrocubanismo —with the sole exception of Wifredo Lam—were all socially racialized as white. Together, the two exhibitions offer a new perspective on the aesthetic contributions of Afro-Cuban art, challenging sanitized and racist constructions of the Cuban nation. They cultivate a space of resistance against the erasure of histories and imaginaries that remain vibrant, transformative, and liberatory.

Elizabeth Pozo Rubio

article_text:
F innish director Hanna Bergholm made a witty and unnerving baby-body-horror movie with her 2022 debut Hatching about a creepy giant egg, a complex, psychologically plausible study of family dysfunction in which the idea of fertility plays an important part. And now … she has given these ideas a retread with this programmatic and unsubtly acted film, a scary movie about a monstrous newborn that is very much less interesting and original than Hatching; the paganism is cliched and the element of black comedy – so often the alibi for not being scary in films like this – is really not all that funny. The face and body of the screeching VFX model devil-baby itself is mostly never shown to the audience, an omission that does not seem disturbing but rather an admission that this prop wouldn’t look convincing in plain sight.

Saga (Seidi Haarla) and her stolid British husband Jon (Rupert Grint) have come to live in Saga’s dilapidated family home in the remote Finnish forest, planning to fix it up so that it can be a lovely place to bring up what they hope will be a big family. (Fixing up this place would in the real world take a couple of years while they lived somewhere else, but they more or less manage it unaided in about two weeks.) Saga is obscurely moved and excited by the vital subterranean forces throbbing in the dark depths of the forest that surrounds the house. They have passionate sex there but the resulting baby is a brutal, hirsute, bloodsucking troll that destroys Saga’s marriage and happiness.

Saga’s unsentimentally down-to-earth mother (nicely played by Pirkko Saisio) is pretty callous, remarking that as a baby Saga was herself a vampiric, nutrition-sucking nightmare. Jon’s parents, played by John Thomson and Rebecca Lacey, are not much more help; the dad is a clergyman who insists on baptising the child in a fireside ceremony with ghastly results. And where is it all leading? Well, to nothing but grief for poor Saga, who unlike pregnant Mia Farrow in Rosemary’s Baby, doesn’t break through to an extended period of calm or acceptance. Some amusing moments, but a disappointment after the excellent Hatching.

article_text:
Territoires atlantiques To the West

A visual drift across the coastline of the French Atlantic seaboard. Territories shaped by waves, tides, the blue economy. Far from a touristic vision, the photographs focus on transitional spaces: marshes, coastal structures, paths, secondary ports, working infrastructures or temporarily deserted places. Human presence appears discreetly. It also reveals itself through its absence.

The project questions our relationship to a coastline that is at once inhabited and exposed, ordinary and singular. Black and white highlights the structure and materiality of the elements. In echo, colour captures the sensitive dimension of the places. A land marked by the power of the elements, as by the history of its uses.

These images are born from an intimate knowledge of these shores, and from a rediscovery.

article_text:
In Bavarian folklore, the gates to the beyond swing wide for twelve nights running, from the winter solstice to Epiphany. Elena Helfrecht has photographed that breach every winter since 2018, alert to the omens her foremothers once read there.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Elena Helfrecht.

Elena Helfrecht grew up in Bavaria, in the Fichtel Mountains, a granite and forested massif in the northeast of the region, pressed hard against the Czech border. Her grandmother and great-grandmother called the nights between solstice and Epiphany the Unternächte. “Life and death, light and darkness blur into a space both dangerous and cathartic,” the photographer writes.

In her family, these nights belong to the women. “Stories are shared, oracles interpreted, and guidance conjured for the uncertain path ahead,” she continues. Her pictures gather up the gestures: a sickle held against a whitewashed door at the back of a cellar; a wedding dress laid out on the snow at the foot of a stump. “Customs convey a sense of meaning and control over things we have little influence over.”

Every winter since 2018, the photographer goes home. She looks there for the weather of those nights and puts the folklore she inherited to the question. In her images the whites run together, rime on the spruces, the breast feathers of geese, the bridal cloth; the black swallows all the rest. Only a frontal light tears the shapes loose from the dark.

No threat ever shows itself outright. The unease rises all the same. “The camera,” she writes, “turns ordinary moments into mystic possibilities.” The book borrows from folk horror, a register bred of rural isolation, old beliefs and village rites, carried to a wide audience by films like The Wicker Man and Midsommar .

In one photograph a Schutzengelbild keeps watch on the wall, the devotional print of the guardian angel steering two children across a broken footbridge, hung by the thousand above German-speaking beds since the 1880s. Below it, the eiderdown smolders as though from spontaneous combustion.

In these customs, smoke cleanses the house and holds the spirits at a distance. “The same fire that keeps a house warm can burn it down,” the Athens publisher notes, matching deed to word: the production credits reserve for Void itself, outside the printing house, the passing of all thousand covers through flame.

The volume, carrying its own scorch mark, will be shelved with the fairy tales, between the Brothers Grimm and Franz Xaver von Schönwerth, collector of the stories of the neighboring Upper Palatinate. We will open it again each year from December 21 on, by the fire.

Unternächte , by Elena Helfrecht, is published by Void (2026). 128 pages, 1,000 copies, burnt hardcover, texts in English and German, €48.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE : The Matrix co-creator Lilly Wachowski has boarded writer-director Molly Ratermann’s murder-bachelorette comedy Making A Bridesmaid as executive producer, with her production company, Anarchists United, also joining the completed feature.

Wachowski’s involvement brings her genre expertise to a film that is said to playfully subvert horror and comedy conventions. The movie will launch worldwide sales via Finn Bruce and Belstone Pictures at the upcoming American Film Market.

“ Making a Bridesmaid is exactly the kind of bold, offbeat genre storytelling that excites us,” said Anarchists United. “Molly Ratermann takes the familiar world of bachelorette culture and turns it into something wildly unpredictable, using horror and dark comedy to explore identity, social expectations and the pressure to belong. We’re excited to support a filmmaker with such a distinctive voice and help bring this unconventional film to audiences worldwide.”

Related Stories

Celine Dion To Perform Paul McCartney's Original Songs For Animated Feature 'High In The Clouds'

A24's Fantasy Epic 'Elden Ring' Heads To AFM As Biggest Movie Ever On Sale At A Market; Amazon Joins Pic Starring Kit Connor

Written, directed, and starring Ratermann, the film is described as “a satirical, ’80s-inspired sleepover from hell that collides the increasingly ubiquitous world of bachelorette culture with the obsessive appeal of true crime.”

Watch on Deadline

The film “follows two outcast sisters, played by Ratermann and Emily Kincaid ( Hard Miles ), who arrive at a picture-perfect bachelorette weekend expecting a celebration — only to discover they have been dropped into a real-life murder game. As the weekend spirals into chaos, the guests are forced to compete for four coveted bridesmaid spots… just to stay alive.”

Produced by 741 Films and Ratermann’s Little Hand Productions, the film was shot on location in Lake Tahoe, California, and has completed post-production ahead of a planned festival run.

“Lilly has built a career telling bold, unconventional stories that challenge the way we see ourselves and the world around us,” said Molly Ratermann. “That’s something I’ve always admired and tried to bring to my own work. Making a Bridesmaid is a pretty outrageous film on the surface, but underneath is a story that questions the roles women are expected to play and the lengths we’ll go to belong. Having Lilly, who’s spent her career pushing against convention, champion this film is an incredible honor and a dream come true.”

The ensemble cast also includes Serra Naiman, Wilder Yari, Alex Sgambati, Gina Su, Maya Butler, April Kelley and Cynthia Aileen Strahan.

Executive producers are Justin Gray, Finn Bruce, Michael D. Whitfield, Sonny Marler, Keith Rosmarin, Darren Cogan and Emily Kincaid.
